strengths: The central question — whether optimization difficulty, rather than statistical accuracy of OPE estimators, is the binding constraint in large-action-space OPL — is important, underexplored, and well motivated for the recommender-system setting.

The oracle-policy analysis (Section 2, Appendix B) is clean and useful: closed-form characterizations of the implicit bias of IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, and PC provide a principled basis for the proposed objective-aware parametrizations, and the reframing of POTEC as an optimization strategy for OffCEM is an insightful observation.

The POTEC vs. OffCEM comparison is a well-designed control: since both target the same asymptotic objective, the performance gap is attributable to optimization rather than statistical bias, directly supporting the paper's thesis.

Concavity (and strong concavity with ℓ2) of PWLL objectives, plus problem-dependent SGA convergence rates, gives a crisp theoretical contrast with the non-concave IPS-based objectives, and the K_eff-based analysis explains why cluster-level decompositions help.

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three datasets with action spaces up to 1M, controlled sweeps over batch size and LR schedules, multi-seed variance analysis, reward-noise ablations, cluster-count and logging-support ablations, pessimistic-variant comparisons, and a smaller-K ablation (Appendix E), with code and artifacts released.

The paper is commendably honest about positioning (PWLL is not novel; objectives are one-step specializations of offline-RL weighted BC), includes a genuine limitations discussion (PWLL is not an estimator, concavity only for linear softmax, dependence on logging support), and impact/ethics are unproblematic.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is limited: Propositions 2.1–2.2 are explicitly adapted from Mei et al. (2020a) and Chen et al. (2019), with the new content being a straightforward lemma that all studied estimators are linear in π; Proposition 3.1 (weighted log-likelihood concavity) is a fairly direct computation. The paper's value rests mainly on synthesis and empirics rather than new theory.

The headline claim 'optimization matters more than estimation' is only partially isolated: most comparisons pit PWLL objectives against IPS-based objectives whose oracle policies differ (e.g., cLPI vs cIPS, RegKL vs ES), so improved performance could partly reflect a different (and favorable) inductive bias rather than better optimization. The POTEC/OffCEM pair is the only true oracle-matched control, and the paper leans heavily on it.

The empirical setup is semi-synthetic with deterministic binary rewards R_i = 1[A_i ∈ H_i] and logging policies constructed from SVD embeddings; this is a benign, well-specified regime. Generalization to noisier, real logged data with model misspecification and worse coverage is asserted but only partially tested (Appendix E.4 noise ablation).

Several key claims (Claims 2.3 and 2.4) are stated formally but validated only empirically, without formal guarantees bounding how much reducing K_eff can help or when it hurts (e.g., excluding optimal actions outside the logging support).

Some evaluation details are thin: the 'validation reward' metric and how counterfactual performance is computed are not fully specified in the main text, some experiments use only 5 seeds, PWLL methods are excluded from the MSE figure for scale reasons (weakening the estimation-vs-optimization comparison), and there are minor errors (e.g., 'IX' for IPS in Appendix E.3).

strengths: The central question — whether optimization or estimation is the binding constraint in OPL for large action spaces — is well-posed and practically relevant, and the paper is unusually candid about its own positioning (PWLL is explicitly not claimed as a novel method; POTEC is reframed rather than claimed as a contribution).

The oracle-policy analysis (Appendix B) is clean and useful: closed-form characterizations of the implicit bias of IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, and PC make the estimator-aware parametrization argument concrete rather than hand-wavy.

The observation that cIPS and cLPI share the same greedy oracle decision rule is a genuinely useful insight: it provides an optimization-friendly route to the cIPS target without changing the asymptotic decision rule.

The empirical stress tests are more thorough than is typical: batch-size and LR-schedule sweeps across three datasets (K up to 1M), 5-seed variance analysis, reward-noise ablations, cluster-count sensitivity, logging-support sensitivity, smaller-K ablations, and pessimism ablations (Appendix E), all with released code.

The comparison of POTEC vs. OffCEM — two methods targeting the same asymptotic objective that diverge in performance — is a clever controlled test isolating optimization as the cause of the gap, and the pessimism ablation (Appendix E.9) preempts a natural objection that statistical regularization alone fixes the problem.
Limitations are honestly discussed: loss of concavity under end-to-end training, dependence of PWLL oracles on the logging policy, and PWLL's unsuitability for evaluation/policy selection.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are explicit adaptations of Mei et al. (2020) and Chen et al. (2019) to linear-in-π objectives; the concavity result (Prop. 3.1) is a straightforward consequence of softmax log-likelihood structure; PWLL objectives are existing weighted-BC/AWR-style updates (LPI, BPR, offline RL methods). The paper acknowledges this, which is honest, but it leaves the contribution resting almost entirely on an empirical diagnosis.

The worst-case theory supports only a weak version of the headline claim. Propositions 2.1/2.2 establish that bad instances exist ('there exist problem instances'), which does not establish that such plateaus/local maxima dominate practical instances, nor that trainability 'dominates estimation accuracy' as a general predictor. The latter is supported only correlationally on the paper's own benchmarks.

The experimental protocol is synthetic in ways that may favor the paper's thesis. Rewards are deterministic (Ri = 1[Ai ∈ Hi]), the logging policy is constructed with top-k0 support from SVD embeddings, and data is preprocessed per Sakhi et al. (2023b). Real logging policies with noisy, overlapping propensities could change the variance landscape that motivates IPS-based estimators in the first place; the paper does not test this regime beyond the noise ablation.

The optimization sweep is confined to batch size and three learning-rate schedules under one optimizer family. The claim that IPS objectives are 'highly sensitive and difficult to tune' would be more convincing with a broader optimizer/tuning budget comparison, or evidence that no reasonable tuning budget rescues them.

The estimator-vs-policy-quality comparison (Figure 3) is asymmetric: PWLL methods are excluded because their MSE 'would distort the scale', so the quantitative estimator-accuracy comparison is restricted to IPS-family methods while the policy-quality comparison includes PWLL. This weakens the 'estimation accuracy does not predict policy quality' argument quantitatively.

Presentation issues: Figures 2, 4, 5, 9, and 14 are dense, small-font, and difficult to read, and key empirical claims (e.g., 'PWLL outperforms IPS-based objectives on all datasets') are asserted from these figures without accompanying tables or significance statistics. Several propositions in the main text (Claims 2.3/2.4) are framed as empirical claims but validated only informally.

The framing that the OPL community has 'neglected' optimization somewhat overstates the gap: Chen et al. (2019) (which the paper itself builds on), POTEC (reframed here as an optimization strategy), and pessimistic regularization already engage with optimization/statistical trade-offs; the paper's contribution is consolidation and diagnosis rather than a fundamentally new insight or method.

strengths: The central question — whether optimization or estimation is the dominant bottleneck in off-policy learning with large action spaces — is important, well-motivated, and largely underexplored relative to the estimator-centric OPL literature.

The effective-action-space (K_eff) framing is a clean and useful lens: it explains why clustered/marginalized estimators (MIPS, OffCEM, PC) still inherit the full softmax landscape unless the parametrization itself is reduced, and it usefully reframes POTEC as an optimization strategy for OffCEM rather than a new estimator.

The oracle-policy analysis (closed-form asymptotic maximizers of each estimator) is a nice diagnostic device that yields concrete, actionable parametrization recommendations (Claim 2.3, Claim 2.4), including the observation that cLPI targets the same greedy decision rule as cIPS while being concave.

The paper is honest and careful in its positioning: PWLL is explicitly not claimed as a novel method, negative results and limitations (PWLL is not a value estimator, concavity only for linear softmax, oracle policies inherit logging-policy coverage issues) are discussed openly, and the same coverage critique is fairly applied to IPS-based methods.

The empirical program is unusually thorough for this area: controlled sweeps over batch size and LR schedules, seed-averaged runs, MSE-vs-policy-quality analysis (Figure 3 vs Figure 2), reward-noise ablations, cluster-count ablations, logging-support ablations, smaller-K ablations, and pessimistic (SVP/PAC-Bayes) baselines in Appendix E. Code is stated to be publicly available.

The seed-variance results (Figure 7) and the POTEC-vs-OffCEM comparison (identical asymptotic objective, different optimization) provide genuinely strong evidence that the performance differences are driven by trainability rather than statistical bias.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is limited: Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are explicitly adapted from Chen et al. (2019) and Mei et al. (2020a), Proposition 3.1 is a direct consequence of the concavity of log-softmax composed with linear scores, and the convergence results in Appendix D are standard applications of Garrigos & Gower theorems. The proofs are correct but confirmatory rather than new.

Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are worst-case existence results ('there exist problem instances'), so the severity of plateaus and exponentially many local maxima in realistic regimes is carried entirely by the empirics; the gap between worst-case constructions and practice is not bridged theoretically.

Claims 2.3 and 2.4 are presented as design principles but are supported only empirically on recommendation-style benchmarks; there is no theory quantifying the trade-off between reducing K_eff and the risk of excluding optimal actions, despite the authors themselves framing this as a 'sweet spot' problem.

The experimental setting is synthetic in a key respect: the logging policy, rewards, and hidden-item splits are constructed by the authors over collaborative-filtering datasets (following Sakhi et al., 2023b), and training is limited to 10 epochs. The headline claim ('optimization matters more than estimation') is demonstrated on this one benchmark family; evidence on real logged feedback or other domains is absent, so generality beyond large-K recommendation bandits is not established.

PWLL objectives (LPI, cLPI, RegKL, BPR) are known techniques (Liang & Vlassis 2022; Rendle et al. 2012; reward-weighted BC in offline RL), and the paper's contribution is a diagnosis rather than a new method. This is defensible but reduces the methodological contribution; the paper would be stronger if the cLPI-vs-cIPS equivalence or a new PWLL variant with better oracle properties were derived.

Some presentation issues: Figure 2 and Figure 9 are dense multi-panel grids that are hard to read; several key results (e.g., the full Claim 2.4 validation across OffCEM/MIPS) rely on figures whose details are hard to verify visually; the 'IX' method mentioned in Appendix E.3 appears without definition.

The MSE analysis (Figure 3) compares estimation quality only among IPS-based methods; PWLL is excluded on the grounds that its MSE is off-scale, so the 'estimation accuracy does not predict policy quality' claim is supported somewhat indirectly rather than with a complete, common-scale comparison.
